title: Perinatal mental illness
blurb: Ask the right questions, recognise severe mental illness and postpartum psychosis as an emergency, refer on time and support safe medicines and feeding (NICE CG192).
question: On day 5 after birth, Ama's partner calls the community midwife: Ama has barely slept for 3 nights, is talking very fast and says the baby has been 'swapped'. She had bipolar disorder before pregnancy. What should the midwife do?

teach.h: Mental health is part of every contact
teach.body: Perinatal mental illness covers mental health problems in pregnancy and the first year after birth, from depression and anxiety to severe mental illness such as bipolar disorder and postpartum psychosis. NICE CG192 asks midwives to recognise that women may not disclose because of stigma or fear that their baby might be taken into care (1.5.1). In plain English: ask kindly at every contact, listen to partners, and know which presentations are emergencies. Psychiatric causes are a leading cause of maternal death in the UK (MBRRACE-UK).

teach.h: Questions at booking and early postnatal (CG192 1.5.4)
head: Tool
Questions
rows: In the past month, often bothered by feeling down, depressed or hopeless? By little interest or pleasure in doing things?
In the last 2 weeks, how often bothered by feeling nervous, anxious or on edge? By not being able to stop or control worrying?
teach.caption: Consider asking both at all later contacts (1.5.8). GAD-2 items score 0-3 each.

steps.label: Positive Whooley or concern
steps.sub: Consider EPDS or PHQ-9 as part of full assessment

steps.label: Severe illness suspected
steps.sub: Refer to a mental health professional

steps.label: Referral made
steps.sub: Assessment within 2 weeks; therapy within 1 month

teach.caption: CG192 1.7.3: assess within 2 weeks of referral and provide psychological interventions within 1 month of initial assessment.

teach.h: Ask about severe mental illness at the first contact
teach.body: At a woman's first contact in pregnancy or after birth, ask about any past or present severe mental illness, past or present treatment by specialist mental health services including inpatient care, and severe perinatal mental illness in a first-degree relative (mother, sister or daughter). Refer all women with current or past severe mental illness to secondary mental health services, preferably a specialist perinatal team, and make sure the GP knows.

rows.label: Who is at higher risk
values: Past severe illness, bipolar, family history

teach.caption: CG192 1.5.11-1.5.12; NHS baby blues guidance. If symptoms last beyond 2 weeks, consider postnatal depression.

head: Medicine
Key point
rows: Not for women of childbearing potential for mental illness; stop if pregnant
Do not offer if planning pregnancy, pregnant or considering breastfeeding
Levels every 4 weeks, weekly from 36 weeks; birth in hospital; stop in labour
Encourage, unless taking carbamazepine, clozapine or lithium
teach.caption: After birth, review the need to start, restart or adjust medication as soon as a woman with severe mental illness is medically stable (1.9.1). Babies exposed to psychotropics need a full neonatal assessment (1.9.2).

items: Ama has a history of bipolar disorder: she is high risk for postpartum psychosis, especially in the first 2 weeks.
Sudden sleeplessness, pressured speech and a belief that her baby has been swapped suggest postpartum psychosis.
The midwife arranges an urgent referral to the specialist perinatal mental health service for assessment within 4 hours, using the crisis pathway.
She makes sure Ama and the baby are not left alone, keeps the partner informed and documents clearly.
If admission is needed, a mother and baby unit allows Ama and her baby to stay together (CG192 1.10.1).

teach.text: Don't label sudden confusion, mania or strange beliefs in the first weeks as 'baby blues'. Blues are mild and settle within about 2 weeks; psychosis is a psychiatric emergency needing assessment within 4 hours of referral (CG192 1.5.12).

items: Whooley and GAD-2 at booking and early postnatal; consider at every later contact.
Positive screen: EPDS or PHQ-9, GAD-7, GP or mental health referral; assess within 2 weeks of referral.
Ask about past or present severe mental illness and first-degree family history; refer to specialist perinatal services.
Postpartum psychosis: be alert in the first 2 weeks; refer for assessment within 4 hours.
No valproate; lithium needs close monitoring; encourage breastfeeding unless on carbamazepine, clozapine or lithium.

summary: You can now screen for depression and anxiety with the CG192 questions, identify women at risk of severe perinatal mental illness, and act on postpartum psychosis as an emergency. You can also outline key medicine safety points and the role of specialist perinatal services and mother and baby units.

A.q: At booking, which pair of questions does NICE CG192 suggest the midwife considers asking to identify possible depression?
A.why: CG192 1.5.4: the 2 depression identification (Whooley) questions about feeling down, depressed or hopeless and loss of interest or pleasure.

whyNot.1: GAD-2 identifies anxiety, not depression, though it is asked alongside.
whyNot.3: CAGE questions screen for alcohol problems, not depression.

A.q: A midwife refers a woman with suspected postpartum psychosis to the specialist perinatal mental health service. Within what time should she be assessed?
A.why: CG192 1.5.12: refer for immediate assessment, within 4 hours of referral.

whyNot.0: 24 hours is too long for a psychiatric emergency.
whyNot.2: 2 weeks is the standard for assessment after a routine mental health referral (1.7.3).
whyNot.3: 72 hours is far too long for suspected postpartum psychosis.

A.q: A woman scores 4 on the GAD-2 at her booking appointment. What does NICE CG192 suggest?
A.why: CG192 1.5.6: a GAD-2 score of 3 or more: consider the GAD-7 for further assessment or referral to the GP (or mental health professional if severe illness is suspected).

whyNot.0: A score of 3 or more prompts further assessment now, not waiting until 28 weeks.
whyNot.1: The threshold is 3, so a score of 4 needs further assessment.
whyNot.3: Inpatient referral is not the response to a positive anxiety screen without severe illness.

B.q: At booking, Sara mentions her sister was admitted with postpartum psychosis. Sara is well. What does this history mean for her care?
options: It is relevant to her sister
Be alert for psychosis after birth
B.why: CG192 1.5.11: if there is a family history of severe perinatal mental illness in a first-degree relative, be alert for possible postpartum psychosis in the first 2 weeks after birth.

whyNot.0: A sister is a first-degree relative, so her history raises Sara's risk.
whyNot.1: First-degree family history needs more than routine care: alertness in the first 2 weeks and a plan.
whyNot.2: Medication is not started because of family history alone in a well woman.

B.q: A woman taking lithium for bipolar disorder is 37 weeks pregnant. How often should her plasma lithium levels be checked now?
B.why: CG192 1.4.37: check lithium levels every 4 weeks, then weekly from 36 weeks.

whyNot.2: Every 2 weeks is not the CG192 schedule.
whyNot.3: A single check is not enough; levels are weekly from 36 weeks and again 12 hours after the last dose in labour.

B.q: A woman taking clozapine for schizophrenia asks about breastfeeding her baby. What does NICE CG192 advise?
B.why: CG192 1.9.8: encourage women with a mental health problem to breastfeed unless they are taking carbamazepine, clozapine or lithium; support her choice of feeding method.

whyNot.0: Clozapine is one of the three medicines where breastfeeding is not encouraged.
whyNot.2: There is no 6-week rule in CG192.
whyNot.3: CG192 does not base the advice on drug levels for clozapine.

C.q: On day 4, Leah's partner says she is not sleeping, is agitated and believes people are watching her through the baby monitor. She has no previous mental illness. What should the midwife do?
options: Diagnose baby blues and review in a week
Ask the GP to see her within 2 weeks
Refer for perinatal assessment within 4 hours
Advise rest and the health visitor
C.why: Sudden onset of symptoms suggesting postpartum psychosis needs referral for immediate assessment within 4 hours (CG192 1.5.12), even with no past history.

whyNot.0: Paranoid beliefs and agitation are not baby blues; delay could be dangerous.
whyNot.1: A 2-week wait is for routine referrals, not suspected psychosis.
whyNot.3: Suspected psychosis needs urgent specialist assessment, not a routine handover.

C.q: Hana takes valproate for bipolar disorder and has just found she is 7 weeks pregnant. What does NICE CG192 advise about her valproate?
options: Continue it with high-dose folic acid
Stop valproate because of fetal risks
C.why: CG192 1.4.29: if a woman already taking valproate becomes pregnant, stop the drug because of the risk of fetal malformations and adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes.

whyNot.0: Folic acid does not make valproate safe; it should be stopped.
whyNot.2: Dose reduction does not remove the risk; CG192 says stop.
whyNot.3: Carbamazepine should not be offered for a mental health problem in pregnancy (1.4.30).

C.q: Bea has a history of severe depression with an inpatient stay 3 years ago. She is well at booking. What should the midwife do?
options: Note it and screen at 28 weeks
C.why: CG192 1.5.10: refer all women with any history of severe mental illness to secondary mental health services, preferably specialist perinatal, and inform the GP.

whyNot.0: A history of severe mental illness needs referral, not just later screening.
whyNot.2: Medicine decisions are made by prescribers after assessment, not advised by the midwife.
whyNot.3: NHS Talking Therapies (formerly IAPT) treats common problems such as mild to moderate depression; a history of severe mental illness goes to secondary or specialist perinatal services (CG192 1.5.10).

reteach.title: Ask, sort, act
reteach.question: If you remember three verbs, can you handle almost any perinatal mental health question: ask, sort, act?

blocks.body: Ask: Whooley and GAD-2 questions, plus past severe illness, specialist treatment and first-degree family history. Sort: mild or moderate problems go to EPDS, PHQ-9 or GAD-7 and usually the GP; severe illness or a history of it goes to specialist perinatal services. Act: suspected postpartum psychosis is an emergency, with assessment within 4 hours of referral.

blocks.text: The 2-week figures are different: baby blues usually go within 2 weeks; psychosis risk is highest in the first 2 weeks; routine referrals are assessed within 2 weeks. Only psychosis carries the 4-hour standard.

explain.body: Whooley questions (depression) and GAD-2 (anxiety) at booking and in the early postnatal period, and consider them at all later contacts. Positive: consider EPDS or PHQ-9, GAD-7, or GP or mental health referral (CG192 1.5.4-1.5.8).

test.q: A woman answers yes to one Whooley question at her 6-week postnatal contact. What is the next step NICE suggests considering?
options: EPDS or PHQ-9 as part of assessment
test.why: CG192 1.5.5: a positive response to either Whooley question: consider EPDS or PHQ-9 as part of a full assessment, or referral to the GP.

whyNot.1: Admission is not indicated by a single positive screening answer.
whyNot.2: Waiting a year leaves possible depression unassessed.
whyNot.3: Medication is not started on a screening answer; full assessment comes first.

explain.body: Ask about past or present severe mental illness, specialist or inpatient treatment, and severe perinatal illness in a mother, sister or daughter. Refer anyone with current or past severe illness to secondary (preferably specialist perinatal) services and tell the GP (CG192 1.5.9-1.5.10).

test.q: Which relative's history of severe perinatal mental illness counts as first-degree under CG192?
test.why: CG192 1.5.9 defines a first-degree relative as mother, sister or daughter.

whyNot.0: An aunt is a second-degree relative.
whyNot.1: A cousin is a third-degree relative.
whyNot.2: A grandmother is a second-degree relative.

explain.body: Sudden onset, usually in the first 2 weeks: confusion, mania, delusions, hallucinations, severe sleeplessness. Refer for immediate assessment within 4 hours. A mother and baby unit is used for admission within 12 months of birth, so mother and baby stay together.

test.q: A woman needs psychiatric admission 3 weeks after birth for postpartum psychosis. Where should she ideally be admitted, according to CG192?
options: A specialist mother and baby unit
test.why: CG192 1.10.1: women who need inpatient care for a mental health problem within 12 months of birth should normally be admitted to a specialist mother and baby unit.

whyNot.0: A general psychiatric ward separates her from her baby and lacks perinatal expertise.
whyNot.1: A postnatal ward cannot safely provide psychiatric inpatient care.
whyNot.3: A medical ward is not appropriate for psychiatric care.

explain.body: Valproate: not for women of childbearing potential for mental illness; stop if pregnant. Carbamazepine: not offered in pregnancy or breastfeeding. Lithium: levels 4-weekly then weekly from 36 weeks; hospital birth; stop in labour, level 12 hours after last dose. Encourage breastfeeding unless on carbamazepine, clozapine or lithium.

items.label: Stop; level 12 h after last dose

test.q: A woman on lithium goes into labour. What does CG192 advise?
options: Stop it and check level at 12 hours
Give it IV for the birth
test.why: CG192 1.4.37: stop lithium during labour and check plasma lithium levels 12 hours after the last dose.

whyNot.0: Increasing the dose risks toxicity, especially with dehydration in labour.
whyNot.1: CG192 advises stopping lithium during labour.
